question: Boss asks if he's "somebody's nephew" or slept with someone to get the role, right after telling him she's impressed with his performance. What's actually happening in that moment?

options.text: His competence gets undercut the second before he can enjoy it
options.note: "I'm impressed" lasted about one sentence before it turned into a question about who he slept with. The compliment wasn't really about him.

options.text: It reduces his hire to something other than merit, out loud, to his face
options.note: He doesn't get to just be good at the job. There's a version of that story where it's not about the work at all, and she just said it out loud.

options.text: There's a power gap doing the work here, not just the words
options.note: She's his boss with the door closed. He can't just say "that's a weird thing to ask" the way he could to a peer.

options.text: She's just making conversation, it's not that deep
options.note: It's a closed-door one-on-one where his boss is asking who he slept with for the job. That's not small talk.

options.text: He should've laughed it off like she wanted
options.note: Going along with it is easier in the room. It's not the same as the comment being fine.

options.text: It's a joke, she said "relax"
options.note: She said relax right after asking. That doesn't undo the question, it just tells him not to react to it.

question: Boss is playing with his tie, then her hand slides down his arm, then she squeezes his bicep, all while talking about how easy or hard she can make things for him. What's the boundary issue?

options.text: Touch is happening without him agreeing to it, at all
options.note: Tie, arm, bicep. Nobody asked. It just kept going.

options.text: It's tied directly to whether he keeps his job
options.note: "How badly do you want to stay" while her hand's on him isn't ambiguous about what's being offered or threatened.

options.text: He physically can't just get up and leave without consequence
options.note: She's his boss, the door's closed, and she just told him she controls how easy or hard things get for him. Leaving isn't free.

options.text: He froze instead of stopping her, so it's partly on him
options.note: Freezing is a completely normal response to this. It's not consent and it's not his fault for not fighting it off.

options.text: It's not a big deal, she didn't actually do anything serious
options.note: Unwanted touch from your boss while she talks about your job security is already the serious part.

options.text: He was too polite about it, that's the real issue
options.note: His tone isn't what made this happen. She did.

question: This happens behind a closed door with nobody else around. There's no bystander in the room. What does ethical bystander behavior even mean in a case like this?

options.text: Building a workplace where people would actually notice a closed-door pattern
options.note: "Stay back after everyone's gone" isn't unusual on its own. It becomes a pattern that colleagues could actually clock, if anyone's watching for it.

options.text: Being someone he could tell afterward without getting a dismissive reaction
options.note: Whether he says anything later depends a lot on what he expects to happen if he does. That's built long before this moment, by how people already respond to things like this.

options.text: Not needing a witness for it to have been wrong
options.note: Ethical bystander behavior usually gets talked about as something that happens in the room. It also includes what happens if nobody was there at all, and whether the response afterward is still taken seriously.

options.text: There's nothing to say here, no one else was around
options.note: True that nobody witnessed it directly. Doesn't mean the concept has nothing to offer once he tells someone.

options.text: He should've recorded it for proof
options.note: Puts the burden of evidence-gathering on him in the moment, on top of everything else happening to him.

options.text: This one's just between the two of them
options.note: Treating it as private is exactly how patterns like this stay invisible to everyone else.

question: He's lying awake that night, still working out what to do, with the choice already narrowed to "go to Monday's meeting." What would an actually supportive response look like if someone knew what happened?

options.text: Believe him without making him prove it first
options.note: It's one person's word against a senior manager's. Starting from doubt makes an already impossible decision worse.

options.text: Let him decide what happens next instead of deciding for him
options.note: Report it, don't report it, quit, stay quiet — huge decisions. Someone taking that decision out of his hands, even to "help," adds another loss of control on top of the first one.

options.text: Take the risk to his job seriously instead of brushing past it
options.note: "She's senior, you're new, they'll believe her" isn't him catastrophizing. It's a realistic read of the situation, and it deserves to be treated as one.

options.text: Tell him to just report it, it's obviously the right move
options.note: Maybe it is the right move eventually. Said flatly like that, it skips over what he's actually weighing and makes his hesitation sound like the problem.

options.text: Tell him it'll blow over if he doesn't make a thing of it
options.note: "Same time Monday" says otherwise. This isn't a one-off that ends on its own.

options.text: Ask him what he was doing alone with her in the first place
options.note: She told him to stay back. That's not a choice he made his way into.
